topics.title: Fontanelle Windows & Standard Views
topics.frontClue: Open fontanelles are acoustic doors: anterior for the survey, posterior and mastoid for the back
topics.corePiece: The anterior fontanelle is the primary window and stays open until roughly 9 to 18 months. A small-footprint sector or microconvex transducer of about 7.5 to 10 MHz is used, with a higher frequency for superficial structures. The standard survey is about six coronal planes, sweeping from the frontal horns through the third ventricle, the caudothalamic grooves, the bodies and trigones of the lateral ventricles, to the occipital lobes, plus five sagittal planes: a midline view showing the corpus callosum, cavum septi pellucidi, third and fourth ventricles and vermis, and parasagittal views of each lateral ventricle and the periventricular white matter. The posterior fontanelle improves views of the occipital horns, where blood layers dependently. The mastoid fontanelle, behind the ear, gives the best view of the posterior fossa: cerebellar hemispheres, fourth ventricle and cisterna magna. Normal choroid plexus is echogenic and lies in the bodies and trigones but never in the frontal or occipital horns.
topics.whyLock: Exams test which window answers which question. Small intraventricular hemorrhage in the occipital horns and posterior fossa hemorrhage are both missed from the anterior fontanelle alone, so the posterior and mastoid views are not optional extras. A classic trap is calling normal choroid plexus in the trigone a clot; the clue is location, because choroid ends at the caudothalamic groove and is absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Another trap: the normal premature brain is smooth with few sulci, so a lissencephalic look at 26 weeks is expected rather than a malformation.

topics.title: Germinal Matrix Hemorrhage Grading
topics.frontClue: Fragile vessels at the caudothalamic groove bleed in tiny preterms: grade I to IV
topics.corePiece: The germinal matrix is a highly vascular, fragile layer beneath the ependyma, most prominent at the caudothalamic groove, that involutes by about 32 to 34 weeks. Infants born before 32 weeks or under 1500 g are at highest risk, and most bleeds occur within the first 72 hours of life. The Papile grading is the exam standard. Grade I is subependymal hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix, seen as an echogenic focus at the caudothalamic groove. Grade II is intraventricular hemorrhage without ventricular dilation. Grade III is intraventricular hemorrhage filling and distending the ventricle. Grade IV, now usually termed periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, is parenchymal hemorrhage adjacent to the ventricle. Acute clot is echogenic; over weeks it retracts, becomes hypoechoic and centrally lucent, and a grade I bleed can evolve into a subependymal cyst while a parenchymal bleed evolves into a porencephalic cyst communicating with the ventricle. Screening is commonly performed at 7 to 14 days in very preterm infants and repeated later.
topics.whyLock: Think of the grades as a story of spreading blood: matrix only, ventricle not dilated, ventricle dilated, then brain tissue. Grade III and IV carry the worst neurodevelopmental prognosis and the highest risk of post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, so follow-up scans watch ventricular size. Traps include calling a bulky normal choroid plexus a grade II bleed, and forgetting that grade IV is a venous infarction rather than simple extension of grade III. A clot that has become hypoechoic is still a clot; echogenicity changes with age, not severity.

topics.title: Periventricular Leukomalacia
topics.frontClue: Bright white matter beside the trigones that later turns into a cluster of holes
topics.corePiece: Periventricular leukomalacia is ischemic necrosis of the white matter in the vascular watershed of the premature brain, typically dorsal and lateral to the external angles of the lateral ventricles, near the trigones and beside the frontal horns. Early on it appears as increased periventricular echogenicity, which is significant when it is equal to or brighter than choroid plexus, is coarse or asymmetric, and persists beyond about 7 to 14 days. Transient normal flaring is homogeneous and less bright than choroid. In roughly 2 to 6 weeks the injured areas may cavitate into multiple small periventricular cysts that do not communicate with the ventricle. Later the cysts collapse and white matter volume loss produces ex vacuo ventriculomegaly with irregular ventricular margins. Risk factors include prematurity, hypotension, hypoxia-ischemia and maternal chorioamnionitis. The classic clinical outcome is spastic diplegia because the fibers to the legs pass closest to the ventricles.
topics.whyLock: The key reasoning is time: echogenicity first, cysts weeks later, then volume loss. That is why a single early scan can miss PVL and why a late scan near term-equivalent age is part of screening. Separate PVL cysts, which sit in white matter and do not connect to the ventricle, from a porencephalic cyst after grade IV hemorrhage, which does. A common trap is labeling ex vacuo dilation as obstructive hydrocephalus; in PVL the head is not enlarging and the ventricles are irregular from tissue loss.

topics.title: Hydrocephalus & Cerebral Doppler RI
topics.frontClue: Measure the ventricles, then let the resistive index tell you whether pressure is rising
topics.corePiece: Ventriculomegaly is enlargement of the ventricles; hydrocephalus implies increased CSF volume under pressure. In neonates the most common cause is post-hemorrhagic obstruction, followed by aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II malformation with myelomeningocele, and Dandy-Walker malformation. On coronal views the frontal horns lose their slit or comma shape and become rounded. Common measurements include the ventricular index (midline to lateral wall of the frontal horn, plotted against gestational age), anterior horn width (diagonal width greater than about 3 mm is enlarged), and the occipital horn or atrium. Dilation of the third and fourth ventricles helps locate the level of obstruction: lateral and third but normal fourth suggests aqueductal stenosis. Spectral Doppler of the anterior cerebral artery gives the resistive index, normally about 0.6 to 0.8 in term neonates. A rising RI, roughly above 0.8 to 0.9, or a marked increase with gentle fontanelle compression, suggests raised intracranial pressure. A low RI below about 0.5 to 0.6 suggests hyperemia and loss of autoregulation after asphyxia, or a high-flow intracranial arteriovenous shunt such as a vein of Galen malformation; by contrast, a patent ductus arteriosus lowers diastolic flow and raises the RI.
topics.whyLock: Pattern the obstruction by which ventricles are dilated, then use Doppler as a physiologic tiebreaker when deciding whether dilation needs a shunt or reservoir. Rounded frontal horns signal pressure, while irregular ventricles with normal head growth suggest atrophy. Traps: RI is affected by a patent ductus arteriosus, heart rate and probe pressure, so compress the fontanelle gently and keep the infant calm. Also, a low RI is not reassuring; after hypoxic injury it can signal loss of autoregulation and a poor outcome.

topics.title: Dandy-Walker & Posterior Fossa Cysts
topics.frontClue: Big fourth ventricle cyst, missing vermis, tentorium pushed up
topics.corePiece: Dandy-Walker malformation is cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle that communicates with an enlarged posterior fossa, combined with hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis and elevation of the tentorium and torcula. The cerebellar hemispheres are splayed apart. Hydrocephalus is present in most cases, and associated anomalies such as agenesis of the corpus callosum and cardiac or chromosomal abnormalities are common. The midline sagittal and mastoid views are best for showing the vermis and the cyst. The differential matters. Mega cisterna magna is an enlarged cisterna magna, often defined as greater than 10 mm, with an intact vermis and normal fourth ventricle. Blake pouch cyst is a herniation of the fourth ventricle roof below an intact but upwardly rotated vermis. Arachnoid cyst is a separate CSF collection with mass effect that does not communicate with the fourth ventricle. In Chiari II malformation, by contrast, the posterior fossa is small and the cisterna magna is effaced.
topics.whyLock: Reason by two questions: is the vermis present, and does the cyst connect with the fourth ventricle? Absent or small vermis plus communication equals Dandy-Walker. Intact vermis and normal fourth ventricle equals mega cisterna magna. A cyst displacing structures without communication equals arachnoid cyst. The classic trap is reading a big posterior fossa as Dandy-Walker without checking the vermis; the opposite trap is forgetting that Chiari II gives a small, crowded posterior fossa rather than a big one.

topics.title: Agenesis of the Corpus Callosum
topics.frontClue: No cavum, parallel ventricles, steer horns and sunray sulci
topics.corePiece: The corpus callosum is the large commissure connecting the hemispheres, seen on the midline sagittal view as a thin hypoechoic C-shaped band bordered by echogenic lines above the cavum septi pellucidi. In agenesis, complete or partial, the sagittal view shows absence of the band and gyri and sulci on the medial hemisphere radiating outward in a sunray or spoke-wheel pattern, with absence of the normal cingulate sulcus. Coronal views show absence of the cavum septi pellucidi, widely separated lateral ventricles whose frontal horns are narrow and pointed laterally in a steer horn or bull horn configuration, and a high-riding third ventricle that may extend between the hemispheres, sometimes forming an interhemispheric cyst. Axial or parasagittal views show parallel lateral ventricles with disproportionate enlargement of the occipital horns, called colpocephaly. Color Doppler may show an abnormal course of the pericallosal artery. Partial agenesis typically spares the anterior portion, the genu, because the callosum develops front to back except for the rostrum.
topics.whyLock: Most exam items hinge on recognizing the cluster of indirect signs, because the absent structure itself is easy to overlook. If the cavum septi pellucidi is missing, ask why: callosal agenesis, septo-optic dysplasia and holoprosencephaly are the main answers. Do not confuse colpocephaly with hydrocephalus; the frontal horns in agenesis are narrow, not ballooned. Also remember the associations, including Dandy-Walker malformation, Chiari II, and syndromes such as Aicardi in girls.

topics.title: Normal Pediatric Organ Sizes
topics.frontClue: Children are not small adults: every normal value scales with age
topics.corePiece: Pediatric normals change with age, so always compare measurements with age-based charts. The neonatal kidney measures about 4 to 5 cm, reaching about 6 cm by 1 year and adult range by adolescence; the two kidneys should be within about 1 cm of each other. The spleen upper limit is roughly 6 cm at 3 months, 7 cm at 1 year, 9 cm at 4 years, 10 cm at 8 years and 11 to 12 cm by 12 to 15 years. The common bile duct upper limit is about 1 mm in neonates, 2 mm in infants to 1 year, 4 mm in older children and about 7 mm in adolescents. The neonatal gallbladder is about 1.5 to 3 cm long after a fast. The neonatal pancreas is relatively large and may be iso- to hyperechoic. Prepubertal ovaries are about 1 cubic cm or less, and the infant adrenal gland is large, about one third of renal size at birth.
topics.whyLock: The registry rarely expects you to memorize every chart value, but it does expect you to recognize which findings are normal for age and which are not. A 3 mm duct is normal in a teenager but dilated in a newborn. A 9 cm spleen is normal at 6 years but enlarged at 6 months. Asymmetry is often more telling than absolute size: a kidney more than about 1 cm smaller than its partner deserves explanation. Trap: the large neonatal adrenal is normal and should not be called a mass.

topics.title: Biliary Atresia
topics.frontClue: Jaundiced infant, tiny or absent gallbladder, echogenic cord above the portal vein
topics.corePiece: Biliary atresia is progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, presenting with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, acholic stools and dark urine in the first weeks of life. It is the most common indication for pediatric liver transplant. Imaging is done after about a 4 hour fast. Key signs: the triangular cord sign, an echogenic triangular or tubular band of fibrous tissue anterior to the right portal vein bifurcation measuring about 4 mm or more in thickness; an absent or small gallbladder, generally under 1.5 cm long, or a gallbladder with an irregular, lobulated wall, the gallbladder ghost triad; failure of the gallbladder to contract after feeding; and an enlarged hepatic artery, about 1.5 mm or more, with subcapsular flow on color Doppler. Intrahepatic ducts are usually not dilated. Associations include the polysplenia or biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with heterotaxy, preduodenal portal vein, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, and choledochal-like cysts in the cystic form. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy shows uptake without excretion to bowel.
topics.whyLock: Timing drives prognosis. The Kasai portoenterostomy works best before about 60 days of age, so the sonographer is part of a race against time. The main differential is neonatal hepatitis, where the gallbladder is usually present and contracts. Trap one: a visible gallbladder does not exclude atresia; look at its size and wall. Trap two: expecting dilated ducts, which are classically absent because the ducts are obliterated rather than obstructed downstream. Always look at the spleen for polysplenia.

topics.title: Choledochal Cyst
topics.frontClue: Cystic mass at the porta that connects to the bile duct, separate from the gallbladder
topics.corePiece: A choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilation of the bile ducts, more common in girls and in Asian populations, often linked to an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction that allows pancreatic juice to reflux into the duct. The classic triad of pain, jaundice and a palpable right upper quadrant mass is present in only a minority. The Todani classification is tested: type I, fusiform or saccular dilation of the extrahepatic duct, is most common at about 80 to 90 percent; type II is a diverticulum of the extrahepatic duct; type III is a choledochocele bulging into the duodenum; type IV is multiple cysts, IVa intra- and extrahepatic and IVb extrahepatic only; type V is Caroli disease, multiple intrahepatic cysts. On ultrasound look for an anechoic cyst in the porta hepatis or pancreatic head that communicates directly with the common hepatic or bile duct, separate from the gallbladder, often with mild intrahepatic duct dilation. Sludge or stones can occur. Long-term risks include cholangitis, pancreatitis and cholangiocarcinoma.
topics.whyLock: The core skill is proving communication with the duct, which separates a choledochal cyst from duplication cysts, hepatic cysts or pancreatic pseudocysts. In infants the crucial differential is cystic biliary atresia, which has a small cyst, a small or abnormal gallbladder and no intrahepatic dilation. In Caroli disease the central dot sign, a portal radicle surrounded by dilated ducts, is a classic clue. Surgical excision with hepaticojejunostomy is preferred because simple drainage leaves the malignant potential behind.

topics.title: Hepatoblastoma & Pediatric Liver Masses
topics.frontClue: Under 3 with high AFP and a calcified solid liver mass: hepatoblastoma
topics.corePiece: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor in children, usually occurring between 6 months and 3 years. It presents as an enlarging abdomen or mass with markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein. Ultrasound shows a large, solid, often well-defined and heterogeneous mass, commonly in the right lobe, which may contain calcifications and septations; check the portal and hepatic veins and the IVC for invasion or tumor thrombus. Associations include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hemihypertrophy, familial adenomatous polyposis and extreme prematurity. Hepatocellular carcinoma occurs in older children and adolescents, often with underlying liver disease. The main benign mimic in young infants is infantile hepatic hemangioma, the most common benign hepatic vascular tumor, presenting before 6 months, with normal or only age-elevated AFP; it may be solitary or multifocal and highly vascular, can cause high-output heart failure and consumptive coagulopathy, and shows a large celiac axis with aortic caliber decreasing below it. Mesenchymal hamartoma is a multicystic benign mass in children under 2.
topics.whyLock: Sort pediatric liver masses by age, AFP and vascularity. Infant under 6 months with heart failure and shunting suggests hemangioma. Toddler with very high AFP and calcified solid mass suggests hepatoblastoma. Teenager with cirrhosis or metabolic disease suggests hepatocellular carcinoma. Multicystic mass in a toddler suggests mesenchymal hamartoma. Trap: AFP is physiologically high in newborns, so it must be compared with age-adjusted values. Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome receive surveillance ultrasound for both hepatoblastoma and Wilms tumor.

topics.title: Pediatric Spleen & Pancreas
topics.frontClue: Toddler with pancreatitis: think trauma first, including abuse
topics.corePiece: The pediatric spleen should be measured against age-based normals; causes of splenomegaly include infection such as mononucleosis, hemolytic anemias, portal hypertension, storage disease and leukemia or lymphoma. Accessory spleens, small round masses isoechoic to spleen near the hilum, are common normal variants. Asplenia and polysplenia occur with heterotaxy syndromes, and a wandering spleen on a long pedicle can torse. In sickle cell disease the spleen often autoinfarcts and becomes small and echogenic, while acute splenic sequestration causes rapid enlargement and anemia. The pediatric pancreas is relatively larger than in adults and can be iso- to hyperechoic compared with liver. In children, pancreatitis is most often caused by blunt trauma, including handlebar injury and non-accidental trauma, followed by drugs, infection, biliary disease, choledochal cyst and congenital anomalies such as pancreas divisum. Sonographic signs are enlargement, decreased echogenicity, peripancreatic fluid and pseudocyst. Cystic fibrosis causes a small, diffusely echogenic, fatty pancreas.
topics.whyLock: Because children rarely have gallstone or alcohol pancreatitis, a young child with pancreatitis, a pseudocyst or a duodenal hematoma should raise concern for injury, including abuse, and findings must be documented carefully. Trap one: calling an accessory spleen a lymph node or mass; matching splenic echotexture is the tell. Trap two: assuming a bright pancreas is abnormal in a neonate. In heterotaxy, look for associated biliary atresia and cardiac anomalies.

topics.title: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
topics.frontClue: Projectile nonbilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks: 3 mm muscle, 15 mm channel
topics.corePiece: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is idiopathic thickening of the pyloric muscle that obstructs gastric outflow. It typically presents between 2 and 12 weeks of age, peaking at 3 to 6 weeks, with projectile nonbilious vomiting, more often in first-born males, sometimes with a palpable olive and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Scan with a high-frequency linear transducer with the infant supine or right side down, often after giving a little glucose water so fluid fills the antrum and pylorus. The standard diagnostic thresholds are a single muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more and a pyloric channel length of 15 to 17 mm or more; a transverse pyloric diameter of about 13 mm or more supports the diagnosis. Signs include the target or doughnut sign in transverse, the cervix sign in longitudinal, the antral nipple sign of redundant mucosa protruding into the antrum, the shoulder sign, and failure of fluid to pass through the canal during several minutes of observation.
topics.whyLock: Measure muscle only, from the outer edge of the hypoechoic muscle to the echogenic mucosa, and do not include mucosa in the wall thickness. Pylorospasm is the main trap: it can mimic stenosis briefly but the measurements fluctuate and fluid eventually passes, so watch over time. An overdistended stomach rotates the pylorus posteriorly; drain or reposition the infant. Bilious vomiting is not pyloric stenosis and should redirect you to malrotation with midgut volvulus. Treatment is pyloromyotomy.

topics.title: Intussusception
topics.frontClue: Toddler with colicky pain and a right-sided target over 2.5 cm
topics.corePiece: Intussusception is telescoping of a proximal bowel segment, the intussusceptum, into a distal segment, the intussuscipiens. The ileocolic type is most common, typically between 3 months and 3 years, peaking at about 6 months to 2 years, and is usually idiopathic, related to lymphoid hyperplasia in the terminal ileum. Classic findings are intermittent colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, a palpable mass and currant jelly stool, though the full triad is uncommon. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear probe is the first-line test. Look for a target or doughnut sign in transverse, often 3 to 5 cm in diameter and usually in the right upper quadrant near the hepatic flexure, and a pseudokidney or sandwich sign in longitudinal. Crescent-shaped mesenteric fat and lymph nodes are drawn into the mass. Transient small bowel to small bowel intussusceptions are smaller, generally under 2.5 cm, lack mesenteric fat, and often resolve spontaneously. Trapped fluid within the mass and absent color flow raise concern for ischemia and reduction failure.
topics.whyLock: Ileocolic intussusception is treated by image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction unless there are contraindications: peritonitis, free air or shock. A pathologic lead point, such as Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst, polyp or lymphoma, is more likely outside the typical age range, especially over about 5 years, so search for it. Trap: a small, peristalsing small bowel target in an otherwise well child is often transient and does not need enema reduction. Scan all four quadrants, because the mass can sit anywhere along the colon.

topics.title: Pediatric Appendicitis
topics.frontClue: Blind-ending, noncompressible tube over 6 mm, plus an appendicolith or hot fat
topics.corePiece: Appendicitis is the most common condition requiring emergency abdominal surgery in children. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test, using graded compression with a high-frequency linear transducer to displace bowel gas, starting at the point of maximal tenderness and tracing the cecum to the appendix base. The inflamed appendix is a blind-ending, aperistaltic, noncompressible tubular structure with an outer diameter greater than 6 mm. Supporting findings include an echogenic shadowing appendicolith, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, hyperemia of the wall on color Doppler, a target appearance in transverse, and adjacent free fluid or reactive nodes. Signs of perforation include loss of the echogenic submucosal layer, a periappendiceal fluid collection or abscess, complex free fluid and decreased wall flow. The appendix can be retrocecal or pelvic, so a full bladder or the left lateral decubitus position may help. In girls, consider ovarian torsion and cysts; in all children, consider mesenteric adenitis and terminal ileitis.
topics.whyLock: The most useful single sign is a noncompressible diameter over 6 mm, but borderline diameters of 6 to 7 mm need secondary signs, especially inflamed fat. Perforation is common in young children because they present late, so the abscess may be the main finding. Traps include calling the terminal ileum the appendix, which is peristaltic and does not end blindly, and losing flow in a gangrenous appendix and mistaking that for normal. A nonvisualized appendix with no secondary signs makes appendicitis less likely but does not exclude it.

topics.title: Malrotation & Midgut Volvulus
topics.frontClue: Bilious vomiting in a newborn: SMV right of SMA, or a whirlpool
topics.corePiece: Malrotation is abnormal rotation and fixation of the midgut during fetal development, leaving a narrow mesenteric base prone to twisting. Midgut volvulus, twisting of the bowel around the superior mesenteric artery, is a surgical emergency that threatens the entire midgut. Most cases present in the first month with bilious vomiting. On ultrasound, the superior mesenteric vein normally lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery. In malrotation the SMV may lie directly anterior or to the left of the SMA, an inverted relationship. In volvulus, color Doppler shows the whirlpool sign: the SMV and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the SMA. Other clues include a dilated, fluid-filled proximal duodenum tapering to a beak, and failure to see the third portion of the duodenum crossing between the aorta and SMA in its normal retroperitoneal position. The upper GI series remains the reference test, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction that fails to cross left of the spine at the level of the duodenal bulb.
topics.whyLock: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and delay can mean loss of the small bowel. A normal SMV and SMA relationship does not fully exclude malrotation, and an abnormal relationship can occur without it, so ultrasound adds to rather than replaces the upper GI series. Visualizing D3 crossing between the aorta and SMA is strong evidence of normal rotation. Trap: confusing bilious vomiting with pyloric stenosis, which is nonbilious. Treatment is the Ladd procedure.

topics.title: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
topics.frontClue: Sick preemie with bright dots in the bowel wall and bubbles in the portal vein
topics.corePiece: Necrotizing enterocolitis is ischemic and inflammatory necrosis of the bowel, most common in premature, low-birth-weight infants within the first weeks of life, usually after feeds have started. It most often involves the terminal ileum and right colon. Clinical signs include feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools and instability. Radiographs remain the first test, but ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer adds information about the bowel wall and perfusion. Findings include bowel wall thickening greater than about 2.5 to 3 mm or, more ominously, wall thinning under about 1 mm; pneumatosis intestinalis, seen as echogenic foci or a granular bright line within the wall; portal venous gas, seen as moving bright echoes in the portal vein and branching echogenic foci in the liver parenchyma; decreased or absent peristalsis; increased wall flow early and absent flow with necrosis; and free fluid. Complex free fluid with echoes or septations and focal fluid collections suggest perforation. Pneumoperitoneum can be seen as echogenic air anterior to the liver.
topics.whyLock: Ultrasound is valued because it shows perfusion and fluid that radiographs cannot, and it can show deterioration before free air appears. Absent wall perfusion, thinning and complex fluid are the findings that push toward surgery. Trap: portal venous gas from umbilical venous catheter flushes can mimic NEC, so correlate clinically. Another trap is assuming normal wall thickness is reassuring; a thinned wall without flow is worse. Use gentle pressure, warmed gel and a fast exam on these fragile infants.

topics.title: Enteric Duplication Cyst
topics.frontClue: A cyst with its own gut signature: bright mucosa inside, dark muscle outside
topics.corePiece: Enteric duplication cysts are congenital cystic or tubular structures that share a wall and blood supply with normal bowel. They can occur anywhere from the mouth to the anus but are most common in the ileum, followed by the esophagus and colon. Many are found prenatally or in early childhood; they may present with vomiting, pain, bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, obstruction, volvulus, or as a lead point for intussusception. The hallmark sonographic finding is the gut signature or double-wall sign: an inner echogenic mucosal layer and an outer hypoechoic muscular layer, sometimes with all five bowel wall layers visible. Peristalsis of the cyst wall may be seen in real time. Contents are usually anechoic but may contain debris or hemorrhage. The differential includes ovarian cyst in girls, choledochal cyst, mesenteric lymphatic malformation, which is thin-walled and often multiseptated, and Meckel diverticulum. Treatment is surgical excision.
topics.whyLock: The gut signature is the answer to most exam questions on this topic, but beware the trap that any cyst with layered echogenic debris can mimic it; true layers are uniform and continuous around the cyst. A thick, layered wall excludes a simple mesenteric cyst. In an infant girl, an ovarian cyst with hemorrhage is a common mimic; finding both ovaries normal helps. Remember that duplication cysts can contain gastric mucosa, which explains bleeding and positive Meckel scans.

topics.title: Neonatal Kidney Appearance
topics.frontClue: Bright cortex and big dark pyramids are normal in a newborn
topics.corePiece: The neonatal kidney looks different from the adult kidney and these differences are frequently tested. Term neonatal kidneys measure about 4 to 5 cm. The renal cortex is often isoechoic or slightly hyperechoic compared with the liver and spleen, especially in premature infants, because of the higher density of glomeruli. The medullary pyramids are relatively large and hypoechoic, creating striking corticomedullary differentiation; they can be mistaken for dilated calyces or cysts. There is little renal sinus fat, so the central echo complex is small. Fetal lobulation, an undulating contour with indentations between lobes, is common and may persist. Transient medullary hyperechogenicity in the first days of life, often attributed to Tamm-Horsfall protein deposition, usually resolves. The adult pattern, with cortex hypoechoic to liver and less prominent pyramids, emerges over the first several months of life. Normal neonatal adrenal glands are large, with a hypoechoic cortex and echogenic central medulla, roughly one third the size of the kidney at birth.
topics.whyLock: The trap is pathologizing normal anatomy. Prominent pyramids arranged around the sinus are not hydronephrosis; true calyceal dilation connects to the renal pelvis. Brightly echogenic cortex can be normal in a neonate but abnormal in an older child, where it suggests medical renal disease. Persistent medullary echogenicity beyond the first weeks suggests nephrocalcinosis, for example from furosemide therapy in premature infants. Postnatal scans for prenatal hydronephrosis are usually delayed beyond about 48 to 72 hours because early dehydration can hide dilation.

topics.title: Hydronephrosis Grading & UPJ Obstruction
topics.frontClue: Big pelvis, dilated calyces, normal ureter and bladder: UPJ obstruction
topics.corePiece: The Society for Fetal Urology system grades hydronephrosis by the appearance of the pelvis, calyces and parenchyma. Grade 0 has no dilation. Grade 1 shows only a slightly visible renal pelvis. Grade 2 shows a dilated renal pelvis with a few calyces visible. Grade 3 shows dilation of the pelvis and all calyces with preserved parenchyma. Grade 4 adds parenchymal thinning. The newer urinary tract dilation, or UTD, classification uses the anteroposterior renal pelvic diameter, with about 10 mm or more abnormal postnatally, plus calyceal dilation, parenchymal thickness and appearance, ureters and bladder. Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is the most common cause of neonatal hydronephrosis. It is more common in boys and on the left and may be bilateral. Ultrasound shows a dilated renal pelvis and calyces that taper abruptly at the UPJ, with a normal-caliber ureter and normal bladder. Causes include intrinsic narrowing and crossing lower pole vessels. Diuretic renography, such as MAG3, assesses function and drainage. Contralateral anomalies are common.
topics.whyLock: Locate the obstruction by following the dilation downstream. Dilated pelvis only implies UPJ; dilated ureter implies the UVJ, reflux or a ureterocele; a thick bladder and bilateral dilation in a boy implies posterior urethral valves. Measure the AP pelvic diameter in transverse at the hilum. Traps: scanning in the first 48 hours can underestimate dilation; an extrarenal pelvis can look dramatic without calyceal dilation; and reflux can mimic obstruction, which is why a VCUG is often paired with ultrasound.

topics.title: Posterior Urethral Valves
topics.frontClue: Boy with a thick bladder, bilateral hydro and a keyhole: valves
topics.corePiece: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra and the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants. They occur only in boys. Prenatally they may cause oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. Postnatal ultrasound shows a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder, often distended or poorly emptying, with a dilated posterior urethra that, together with the bladder, creates the keyhole sign. Bilateral hydroureteronephrosis is typical, and the kidneys may be small, echogenic and contain cortical cysts, indicating renal dysplasia. Pressure pop-off mechanisms, such as a urinoma, perirenal fluid, urinary ascites or a large bladder diverticulum, may protect one kidney. The posterior urethra can be imaged by a transperineal approach during voiding. The voiding cystourethrogram is the diagnostic test, showing a dilated posterior urethra with an abrupt caliber change at the valve. Treatment is endoscopic valve ablation, but many boys develop chronic kidney disease.
topics.whyLock: Reason from anatomy: an obstruction below the bladder dilates everything above it, so expect a thick bladder plus bilateral ureters and pelves. Unilateral dilation does not fit valves unless there is a pop-off or reflux into one side. Renal parenchymal echogenicity and cysts predict poorer renal outcome, so describe them. Trap: in a girl with similar findings, think of neurogenic bladder or urogenital sinus anomalies instead. Prune belly syndrome can mimic valves but usually has a large, smooth-walled bladder.

topics.title: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney vs ARPKD
topics.frontClue: Grapes that do not connect, versus two huge bright kidneys
topics.corePiece: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a nonfunctioning, dysplastic kidney replaced by multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size with no normal renal parenchyma and no central renal pelvis. It is usually unilateral and found prenatally or as a neonatal flank mass. Nuclear medicine shows no function. The contralateral kidney has a high rate of anomalies, about 20 to 40 percent, especially vesicoureteral reflux and UPJ obstruction, and usually shows compensatory hypertrophy. Most MCDKs involute over time and are followed with ultrasound. Bilateral MCDK is lethal. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease presents with bilaterally enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, because innumerable tiny dilated collecting ducts, too small to resolve individually, create many interfaces. A thin hypoechoic peripheral rim of compressed cortex may be seen, and with high-frequency linear transducers small cysts of 1 to 2 mm may be visible. ARPKD is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension, inversely related to renal severity, and prenatal oligohydramnios with Potter sequence.
topics.whyLock: For MCDK, the decisive question is whether the cysts communicate with a central pelvis. In severe hydronephrosis, dilated calyces connect to a medial pelvis; in MCDK, the largest cyst is usually not central and cysts do not connect. For ARPKD, reason about size: very large, bright kidneys in a neonate mean ARPKD, whereas autosomal dominant disease usually shows larger discrete cysts later in life. Always image the liver and spleen in ARPKD, and always scrutinize the contralateral kidney in MCDK.

topics.title: Wilms Tumor
topics.frontClue: Preschooler with a big flank mass that grows from the kidney with a claw sign
topics.corePiece: Wilms tumor, or nephroblastoma, is the most common renal malignancy of childhood, with a peak at about 3 to 4 years. It usually presents as an asymptomatic, large flank or abdominal mass, sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. Sonographically it is a large, solid, well-circumscribed mass arising from the kidney, with heterogeneous echogenicity from hemorrhage, necrosis and cystic areas. The claw sign, renal parenchyma wrapping around the mass, confirms renal origin. Calcification is uncommon, seen in about 10 to 15 percent. Wilms tumor displaces adjacent vessels rather than encasing them, and it tends to invade the renal vein and IVC as tumor thrombus, which may extend into the right atrium; scan the renal vein, IVC and heart. Look also for the contralateral kidney, because about 5 to 10 percent are bilateral, and for liver metastases and lymph nodes. Associations include WAGR syndrome, Denys-Drash syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hemihypertrophy, which warrant surveillance ultrasound, often every 3 months until about age 7 or 8. Nephroblastomatosis consists of precursor nephrogenic rests.
topics.whyLock: The exam loves the Wilms versus neuroblastoma comparison. Wilms: older preschooler, arises from the kidney with a claw sign, rarely calcified, displaces vessels, invades veins, stays on one side of midline. Neuroblastoma: younger, suprarenal, frequently calcified, encases and lifts vessels, crosses midline. Trap: the neonate with a solid renal mass more likely has mesoblastic nephroma than Wilms. Avoid vigorous palpation, which could rupture the tumor; gentle scanning is the rule.

topics.title: Neuroblastoma
topics.frontClue: Toddler with a calcified suprarenal mass that wraps around the aorta and crosses midline
topics.corePiece: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor of neural crest cells and the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and the most common malignancy in infancy. Most children are under about 2 years at diagnosis, and nearly all under 5 or 6. The adrenal medulla is the most common origin, followed by paraspinal sympathetic ganglia in the abdomen, chest, neck and pelvis. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous, poorly marginated solid suprarenal mass that displaces the kidney inferiorly and laterally without a claw sign. Calcifications are present in most cases, roughly 85 to 90 percent, and appear as echogenic foci with shadowing. The tumor characteristically encases and elevates vessels such as the aorta, IVC, celiac axis and SMA without invading their lumens, and it often crosses the midline. Urine catecholamine metabolites, vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid, are elevated. Metastases go to bone, bone marrow, liver and skin; in infants under 18 months, stage MS (formerly 4S) disease may massively infiltrate the liver and often regresses. Periorbital bone metastases cause raccoon eyes.
topics.whyLock: Reason by the vessel rule: neuroblastoma surrounds vessels, Wilms pushes them. Add age, calcification and origin and you can answer nearly every comparison question. Cystic neuroblastoma in a newborn can mimic adrenal hemorrhage; follow-up shows hemorrhage shrinking and losing echoes while tumor persists or grows, and tumor may show internal flow. Trap: forgetting to examine the liver, which can be diffusely infiltrated in infants rather than showing discrete nodules, so survey it fully.

topics.title: Neonatal Adrenal Hemorrhage
topics.frontClue: Big baby after a hard delivery with a suprarenal mass that turns from bright to cystic
topics.corePiece: The neonatal adrenal gland is large and vascular, which makes it vulnerable to hemorrhage. Risk factors include birth trauma, large-for-gestational-age infants, infants of diabetic mothers, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis and coagulopathy. It occurs more often on the right, about 70 percent, and is bilateral in about 10 percent. Infants may present with a flank mass, anemia, prolonged jaundice or, rarely, adrenal insufficiency. The ultrasound appearance evolves with time. Acute hemorrhage is a solid-appearing, echogenic suprarenal mass. Over about 1 to 2 weeks it liquefies, becoming mixed and then hypoechoic or anechoic and cystic, and it shrinks progressively. Weeks to months later it may calcify, leaving a small echogenic, shadowing focus. A key feature is absence of internal blood flow on color Doppler. The left adrenal hemorrhage may be associated with left renal vein thrombosis because the left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein; look for an enlarged kidney and thrombus. Management is conservative with serial ultrasound.
topics.whyLock: Serial ultrasound is the diagnostic tool. Hemorrhage evolves and shrinks over days to weeks; neuroblastoma persists or grows and may show internal vascularity and elevated urine catecholamines. Reason from the timeline: a mass that was bright last week and is cystic and smaller this week is a resolving hemorrhage. Traps include calling an acute echogenic hemorrhage a solid tumor on a single scan, and forgetting to check the renal vein on the left side.

topics.title: Neonatal & Prepubertal Uterus and Ovaries
topics.frontClue: Hormones shape the uterus: bulbous at birth, tube-shaped in childhood, pear-shaped after puberty
topics.corePiece: Uterine shape changes with hormonal exposure. In the newborn, maternal and placental hormones stimulate the uterus, which measures about 3.5 cm long, and is prominent and often spade-shaped, with the cervix larger than or equal to the fundus, and a visible echogenic endometrial stripe, sometimes with a little fluid. Within a few months this stimulation fades. The prepubertal uterus is small, about 2.5 to 4 cm, tubular or spade-shaped, with the cervix equal to or larger than the fundus, a fundus to cervix ratio of about 1:1 or less, and a thin or invisible endometrium. After puberty, the fundus becomes larger than the cervix, with a ratio of about 2:1 to 3:1, and the uterus is pear-shaped. Ovaries are imaged through a full bladder. Prepubertal ovarian volume is usually about 1 cubic cm or less; small follicles are normal at all ages. Neonatal ovarian cysts are common, from maternal hormone stimulation. Cysts over about 2 cm are significant, and those over about 4 to 5 cm carry a risk of torsion.
topics.whyLock: The exam asks you to match uterine morphology to hormonal status. An adult-shaped uterus or thick endometrium in a young child implies estrogen exposure, so consider precocious puberty or an estrogen-producing tumor. Ovarian volume above about 1 to 2 cubic cm in a young girl is also a puberty marker. Traps: calling small follicles pathologic, or forgetting that a large neonatal ovarian cyst may lie in the upper abdomen rather than the pelvis. A fluid-debris level in a neonatal cyst suggests hemorrhage or prior torsion.

topics.title: Ovarian Torsion
topics.frontClue: Big, swollen ovary with peripheral follicles: flow does not rule out torsion
topics.corePiece: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, on its vascular pedicle, compromising venous and lymphatic outflow and later arterial inflow. In children it can occur with a normal ovary because the adnexal ligaments are long and mobile, but lead points such as cysts and mature cystic teratoma are common. It is more frequent on the right. Patients present with acute, often intermittent pelvic or lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. The most consistent sonographic finding is unilateral ovarian enlargement, markedly larger than the contralateral ovary, often several times its volume. The stroma becomes edematous and heterogeneous, and follicles are pushed to the periphery, the string of pearls appearance. The ovary may be displaced midline or above the uterus. Free fluid is common. The twisted pedicle may show a whirlpool sign. Doppler findings are variable: arterial and even venous flow may be preserved because of the dual ovarian and uterine arterial supply, so presence of flow does not exclude torsion.
topics.whyLock: The registry trap is the flow trap. Asymmetric enlargement plus peripheral follicles in a child with pain should prompt urgent surgical consultation even if color Doppler shows flow. Compare volumes of both ovaries. Always look for a lead mass, such as a teratoma with an echogenic plug and shadowing. Right-sided torsion can mimic appendicitis, so the pelvis should be examined in girls with right lower quadrant pain. Detorsion saves the ovary even when it looks dark and congested at surgery.

topics.title: Hydrometrocolpos
topics.frontClue: Midline cystic mass behind the bladder filled with echoes: a blocked vagina
topics.corePiece: Hydrocolpos is fluid distension of the vagina, and hydrometrocolpos is distension of both the vagina and uterus, caused by vaginal outflow obstruction. Causes include imperforate hymen, the most common, transverse vaginal septum, vaginal atresia, and more complex urogenital sinus or cloacal malformations. It presents in two peaks. In the neonate, maternal estrogen stimulates secretions that accumulate behind the obstruction, producing hydrometrocolpos and a lower abdominal mass. At menarche, menstrual blood accumulates, producing hematocolpos or hematometrocolpos with cyclic pain and primary amenorrhea. Ultrasound shows a midline, tubular or pear-shaped cystic mass posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum, often with low-level echoes or a fluid-debris level, with the small uterus perched on top or itself distended. The mass can compress the bladder and ureters, causing hydronephrosis. Transperineal imaging helps measure the thickness of the obstructing tissue. Associated renal and anorectal anomalies should be sought.
topics.whyLock: Location is the key. A midline cystic mass between bladder and rectum in a girl is vaginal until proven otherwise; follow it up into the uterus to prove it. Separate it from ovarian cysts, which are lateral or upper abdominal and surrounded by ovarian tissue, and from anterior sacral meningocele or sacrococcygeal teratoma, which arise posterior to the rectum. Trap: in a newborn with a pelvic mass and a single perineal opening, think cloacal malformation and check the kidneys and spine.

topics.title: Testicular Torsion
topics.frontClue: Teenager with sudden scrotal pain and a testis with no flow: the clock is ticking
topics.corePiece: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, cutting off venous outflow and then arterial inflow. It has two peaks. Neonatal extravaginal torsion occurs when the entire testis and tunica twist before fixation, often prenatally, and the testis is usually already infarcted. Intravaginal torsion, the more common form, occurs in adolescents, peaking around 12 to 18 years, due to the bell clapper deformity, in which the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis completely and leaves it free to rotate. Presentation is sudden severe pain, nausea, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex. Ultrasound shows absent or markedly decreased intratesticular flow compared with the normal side. Early, the testis may look normal in grayscale; later it enlarges and becomes heterogeneous and hypoechoic, with a reactive hydrocele and scrotal wall thickening. The spermatic cord may show a whirlpool sign or a twisted, enlarged knot above the testis. Salvage is about 90 percent or more within 6 hours and falls sharply after 12 to 24 hours.
topics.whyLock: Always compare with the asymptomatic side using identical settings, ideally in a side-by-side transverse view. Optimize for slow flow: low PRF and scale, low wall filter, high color gain, and power Doppler. Prepubertal testes have little flow normally, which makes comparison essential. Traps: partial torsion or spontaneous detorsion may show preserved or even increased flow, so the whirlpool cord is the deciding clue. Imaging must never delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.

topics.title: Torsion of the Appendix Testis
topics.frontClue: Blue dot at the upper pole and a normal testicular flow: appendage torsion
topics.corePiece: The appendix testis is a small vestigial remnant of the Mullerian duct at the upper pole of the testis, near the epididymal head; the appendix epididymis is a remnant of the Wolffian duct. Torsion of one of these appendages is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys, peaking around 7 to 12 years. Pain is often more gradual and localized to the upper pole, and a small tender bluish nodule, the blue dot sign, may be seen through the skin. Ultrasound shows a round nodule adjacent to the upper pole of the testis or epididymal head, often greater than about 5 mm, which may be hyperechoic, hypoechoic or heterogeneous and shows no internal flow, with surrounding hyperemia of the epididymis and scrotal tissues, a reactive hydrocele and skin thickening. Intratesticular flow is normal. Management is conservative with analgesia. Epididymitis, the other main differential, shows an enlarged, hypoechoic, hyperemic epididymis; in prepubertal boys it should prompt a search for urinary tract anomalies.
topics.whyLock: The decisive finding is normal flow in the testis itself. That changes management from emergency surgery to rest and analgesia. Peripheral hyperemia around the appendage can be misread as epididymitis, so look carefully at the upper pole for an avascular nodule. Trap: assuming increased flow always means infection; it may be a reactive response to appendage torsion or a detorsed testis. Age helps too: torsed appendages are typical before puberty, testicular torsion peaks in adolescence.

topics.title: Undescended Testis
topics.frontClue: Empty scrotum: look first in the inguinal canal, and remember small and dark
topics.corePiece: Cryptorchidism, failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum, affects about 3 percent of term boys and up to about 30 percent of premature boys, and spontaneous descent reduces this to about 1 percent by 1 year. It is more often unilateral and more common on the right. About 80 percent of undescended testes are palpable, and most lie in the inguinal canal or just beyond the external inguinal ring; others are intra-abdominal or ectopic. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear probe searches from the scrotum through the inguinal canal to the internal ring. The undescended testis is typically smaller and slightly hypoechoic compared with the normal testis, oval, with a visible mediastinum testis, which helps separate it from a lymph node. A retractile testis can be manipulated into the scrotum and is normal. Complications include infertility, testicular malignancy, especially seminoma, with a risk several times higher, torsion and associated inguinal hernia. Orchiopexy is recommended by about 6 to 18 months.
topics.whyLock: Ultrasound is good at finding inguinal testes but cannot reliably exclude an intra-abdominal testis, which is why current guidelines do not require routine ultrasound before referral and laparoscopy is used for nonpalpable testes. The mediastinum testis is the discriminator from lymph nodes. Trap: calling a small testis atrophic without comparing echotexture; another trap is missing bilateral nonpalpable testes in a newborn, which demands evaluation for disorders of sex development such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

topics.title: Hydrocele & Pediatric Scrotal Masses
topics.frontClue: Prepubertal testicular tumors are mostly teratoma or yolk sac; check AFP
topics.corePiece: A hydrocele is fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, appearing as anechoic fluid surrounding the anterolateral testis. Congenital hydroceles are common in infants and usually resolve by 1 to 2 years. A communicating hydrocele connects with the peritoneum through a patent processus vaginalis, varies in size during the day and may accompany an indirect inguinal hernia, which appears as bowel with peristalsis or echogenic omentum in the inguinal canal or scrotum; incarceration shows fluid-filled, aperistaltic bowel with thickened wall. Reactive hydroceles accompany torsion, infection and trauma. Intratesticular masses in prepubertal boys differ from adults: mature teratoma and yolk sac tumor are the most common primary tumors, and yolk sac tumor raises alpha-fetoprotein. Epidermoid cyst shows an onion ring or target appearance without flow. Leukemia and lymphoma infiltration cause diffuse or focal hypoechoic, hypervascular enlargement, often bilateral, since the testis is a sanctuary site. Bilateral hypoechoic masses near the mediastinum in congenital adrenal hyperplasia are testicular adrenal rests.
topics.whyLock: Separate extratesticular from intratesticular first: most extratesticular lesions are benign, most intratesticular solid masses need further workup. In prepubertal boys, many tumors are benign, so testis-sparing surgery may be considered. Traps: forgetting to scan the inguinal canal for a hernia when a hydrocele is large, and missing leukemic relapse because the enlarged testis was attributed to orchitis. Paratesticular rhabdomyosarcoma is an important extratesticular malignancy in children and adolescents, so a solid mass outside the testis is not automatically benign.

topics.title: Neonatal Spine Screening & Conus Level
topics.frontClue: Before the posterior arches ossify, the conus should end at or above L2-L3
topics.corePiece: The infant spine can be imaged sonographically until the posterior elements ossify, best in the first 3 months and usually possible until about 6 months. A high-frequency linear transducer is used with the infant prone or in a lateral decubitus position, often with a pillow under the abdomen to flex the spine. Indications include cutaneous stigmata above the gluteal crease such as a hair tuft, hemangioma, skin tag, subcutaneous mass, or a dimple larger than about 5 mm or more than about 2.5 cm from the anal verge, and anorectal malformations. The normal cord is hypoechoic with an echogenic central echo complex, tapering to the conus medullaris, which should lie at or above the L2-L3 disc space. A conus at L3 or below is abnormal. The filum terminale should be under about 2 mm thick, and cord and nerve roots should show normal pulsatile motion. Levels are counted from the last rib-bearing vertebra, T12, or upward from the lumbosacral junction.
topics.whyLock: Level counting is the error-prone step. Use two methods, counting up from the sacrum and down from T12, and document with labeled images. A borderline conus at the L3 level, especially in a premature infant, may simply reflect immaturity and can be rescanned. Traps: a normal ventriculus terminalis, a small cystic dilation of the central canal at the conus, should not be called a syrinx, and a filar cyst is also a normal variant. Lack of cord motion is a functional sign of tethering.

topics.title: Tethered Cord
topics.frontClue: Low-lying conus, fat in a thick filum, and a cord that does not move
topics.corePiece: Tethered cord syndrome occurs when the spinal cord is abnormally anchored caudally, preventing normal ascent and causing traction injury as the child grows. Causes include a thickened or fatty filum terminale, intradural lipoma, lipomyelomeningocele or lipomyelocele, diastematomyelia (split cord), dermal sinus tract and previous myelomeningocele repair. On ultrasound, findings include a conus at or below L3, a filum terminale thicker than about 2 mm, an echogenic filum from fat infiltration, an echogenic intradural lipoma in continuity with subcutaneous fat, a cord lying dorsally against the posterior canal, and reduced or absent pulsatile motion of the cord and nerve roots. A dermal sinus appears as a hypoechoic tract running from the skin toward the canal. Open defects such as myelomeningocele are usually obvious clinically and associated with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus. Clinically, tethering can cause bladder dysfunction, leg weakness, foot deformities, scoliosis and back pain. MRI confirms the anatomy before surgical untethering.
topics.whyLock: The combination of position and motion is what matters. A low conus with absent pulsation is highly suggestive, while a borderline position with normal motion may simply be followed. Fat is echogenic, so a bright, thick filum is a reliable clue. Trap: closed defects under intact skin are easy to miss without stigmata, which is why cutaneous markers drive screening. Another trap is forgetting the association of myelomeningocele with Chiari II malformation, which links spine and brain imaging.

topics.title: Graf Alpha Angle
topics.frontClue: Straight iliac line, bony roof: 60 degrees or more is a mature hip
topics.corePiece: The Graf method uses a static coronal image of the infant hip in lateral decubitus with a linear transducer. The standard plane must show a straight, horizontal iliac line parallel to the transducer, the lower limb of the ilium in the acetabular fossa, and the acetabular labrum. Three lines are drawn: the baseline, the bony roof line and the cartilaginous roof line. The alpha angle, between the baseline and the bony roof line, measures the depth of the bony acetabulum. The beta angle, between the baseline and the cartilaginous roof, measures cartilage coverage. Type I hips have an alpha angle of 60 degrees or more. Type IIa, 50 to 59 degrees, is physiologically immature under 3 months; type IIb is the same range after 3 months. Type IIc is 43 to 49 degrees with beta under 77, and type D has beta over 77, a decentering hip. Type III and IV are under 43 degrees and dislocated.
topics.whyLock: Technique dominates: an oblique plane that does not show a straight iliac line gives a falsely low or high alpha angle, so the plane comes first, then the measurement. Timing matters because laxity is normal in the first weeks; screening of at-risk infants is typically performed around 4 to 6 weeks of age. Risk factors include breech presentation, female sex, family history, first-born status, oligohydramnios and tight swaddling. Trap: calling a type IIa hip under 3 months dysplastic rather than immature and due for follow-up.

topics.title: Femoral Head Coverage & Dynamic Hip Stress
topics.frontClue: At least half of the femoral head should sit under the bony acetabulum
topics.corePiece: Femoral head coverage, popularized by Harcke and Morin, is measured on the same coronal view used for Graf. Draw the iliac line and measure the portion of the femoral head diameter lying medial to it, beneath the bony acetabulum, as a percentage of the total diameter. Coverage of 50 percent or more is normal; roughly 40 to 50 percent is borderline or immature, especially in young infants; less than about 40 percent suggests subluxation, and very low coverage suggests dislocation. The dynamic examination uses a transverse flexion view with the hip flexed 90 degrees. In a normal hip the femoral head sits deep in the acetabulum between the pubis and ischium, forming a U shape. A gentle Barlow stress, adduction with posterior pressure, tests for posterior subluxation or dislocation, while the Ortolani maneuver relocates a dislocated hip. The femoral head is initially unossified, hypoechoic with speckled echoes; the ossific nucleus appears between about 2 and 8 months and eventually shadows the acetabulum, limiting ultrasound beyond about 6 months.
topics.whyLock: Static coverage and dynamic stability answer complementary questions: Is the hip shallow, and is it unstable? Many immature hips stabilize by themselves, so serial imaging is common. Stress testing during Pavlik harness treatment is done only with physician direction, often without removing the harness. Trap: measuring coverage in an oblique plane exaggerates the result. After the ossific nucleus enlarges, radiographs replace ultrasound, typically after about 4 to 6 months of age.

topics.title: Hip Joint Effusion
topics.frontClue: Limping child: measure the anterior recess, but fluid alone cannot tell sepsis from synovitis
topics.corePiece: The hip joint effusion exam is an anterior approach with the child supine, the leg in neutral or slight external rotation, and a linear transducer placed parallel to the femoral neck. The anterior joint recess is measured from the anterior cortex of the femoral neck to the outer margin of the joint capsule. A distance greater than about 5 mm, or a difference of 2 mm or more compared with the asymptomatic side, indicates an effusion. Always scan both hips. Transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain and limp in children aged roughly 3 to 10 years, often after a viral illness, and resolves with rest. Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency that can destroy the joint; clinical predictors include fever over 38.5 degrees C, refusal to bear weight, elevated ESR and elevated white blood cell count. Ultrasound can guide aspiration of the joint for diagnosis. Other causes of limp include Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents, osteomyelitis and injury.
topics.whyLock: The registry trap is believing that the appearance of fluid distinguishes septic arthritis from transient synovitis. Echogenic or anechoic, with or without synovial hyperemia, the fluid cannot reliably make that call; clinical criteria and aspiration do. A negative ultrasound with no effusion makes septic arthritis of the hip unlikely. Compare sides with the same technique and measure perpendicular to the femoral neck. Children with suspected osteomyelitis may show subperiosteal fluid next to the metaphysis.

topics.title: Pediatric Soft Tissue Masses
topics.frontClue: Lump in a child: cystic, vascular or solid, and how fast is it flowing?
topics.corePiece: Ultrasound is the first-line test for superficial pediatric masses. Infantile hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy; it appears after birth, grows rapidly during a proliferative phase in the first months and involutes over years. In proliferation it is a well-defined solid mass with high vessel density, arterial and venous flow and low resistance, without arteriovenous shunting; involution brings increasing fat and decreasing flow. Vascular malformations are present at birth and grow with the child. Venous malformations are compressible hypoechoic channels with slow or no detectable flow and may contain echogenic shadowing phleboliths. Lymphatic malformations are multiloculated cystic masses with septations, fluid-fluid levels and no internal flow except in septa, common in the neck and axilla. Arteriovenous malformations show high-flow vessels without a soft tissue mass. Other common masses include lipomas, abscesses with peripheral hyperemia, foreign bodies, ganglion cysts and pilomatricoma, a calcified superficial nodule. Concern for malignancy, such as rhabdomyosarcoma, rises with size over about 5 cm, deep location, growth and chaotic vascularity.
topics.whyLock: Organize by internal content and flow. Cystic with septations suggests a lymphatic malformation; compressible with phleboliths suggests a venous malformation; solid with dense flow in an infant suggests hemangioma; high-flow vessels without mass suggest AVM. The timeline matters: hemangiomas are not usually present at birth and then grow and fade, while malformations are present at birth and grow proportionally. Trap: calling an atypical solid, hypervascular mass in an older child a hemangioma; that needs MRI and possibly biopsy.

topics.title: Fibromatosis Colli
topics.frontClue: Infant with torticollis and a fusiform, thickened sternocleidomastoid that moves with the muscle
topics.corePiece: Fibromatosis colli, also called pseudotumor of infancy, is benign fibrous thickening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and a common cause of congenital muscular torticollis. It presents at about 2 to 8 weeks of age with a firm neck mass and head tilt toward the affected side, with the chin turned away. Risk factors include birth trauma, breech presentation, forceps delivery and primiparity, and it can be associated with developmental dysplasia of the hip. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer shows fusiform enlargement of the sternocleidomastoid, usually in the lower two thirds, with variable echogenicity, isoechoic, hyperechoic or heterogeneous, and preserved muscle fibers. The mass moves with the muscle and is contained within it, with no separate discrete lesion, no adjacent lymphadenopathy, no fluid collection and no calcification. Comparison with the contralateral normal muscle is essential, in both longitudinal and transverse planes. Treatment is physical therapy with stretching, and most cases resolve within months; a few require surgical release.
topics.whyLock: The diagnosis rests on proving that the mass is the muscle itself. If the lesion lies outside the sternocleidomastoid or displaces it, think of lymph nodes, branchial cleft cysts, lymphatic malformation or neuroblastoma instead. The correct answer is almost never biopsy, because the history and imaging are characteristic. Trap: calling the enlarged muscle a mass because of heterogeneous echogenicity. Because of shared risk factors, these infants are often screened for hip dysplasia.

topics.title: Thyroglossal Duct & Branchial Cleft Cysts
topics.frontClue: Midline and moves with the tongue, or lateral at the angle of the jaw
topics.corePiece: Thyroglossal duct cyst is the most common congenital neck mass in children. It forms along the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum to the lower neck and typically lies in the midline or just off midline, near the hyoid bone, often embedded in the infrahyoid strap muscles. It classically moves upward with swallowing or tongue protrusion. On ultrasound it may be anechoic with posterior enhancement but is often pseudosolid, with internal echoes from proteinaceous fluid or infection. Before surgical removal by the Sistrunk procedure, which includes the central hyoid, confirm a normal thyroid gland in its usual location, because ectopic thyroid tissue may be the only functioning thyroid. Branchial cleft cysts arise from incomplete obliteration of the branchial apparatus. The second branchial cleft cyst accounts for about 90 to 95 percent and lies at the angle of the mandible, anteromedial to the sternocleidomastoid, posterior to the submandibular gland and lateral to the carotid vessels. It is usually anechoic with thin walls but can become complex when infected.
topics.whyLock: Location is the most powerful discriminator: midline means thyroglossal, lateral at the mandibular angle means second branchial cleft. Both may look solid because of debris, so look for posterior enhancement and absence of internal flow. The most tested pearl is to document the normal thyroid before thyroglossal cyst excision. Trap: a solid component with flow within a thyroglossal cyst in an older child raises concern for papillary thyroid carcinoma arising in the cyst.

topics.title: Cervical Lymphadenopathy
topics.frontClue: Oval with a bright hilum is reactive; round, hilum-less and chaotic flow worries you
topics.corePiece: Cervical lymph nodes are very common in children and most are reactive to viral or bacterial infection. A normal or reactive node is oval, with a long to short axis ratio greater than about 2, a hypoechoic cortex, an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar vascularity on color Doppler. A short-axis diameter over about 1 cm is generally considered enlarged, though larger reactive nodes are common in the upper neck. Suppurative lymphadenitis, often from Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococcus, produces an enlarged tender node that may liquefy into an abscess with central hypoechoic or anechoic fluid, no internal flow, peripheral hyperemia and surrounding echogenic inflamed fat; ultrasound identifies drainable collections and guides aspiration. Atypical mycobacterial infection causes matted nodes with necrosis and overlying skin involvement. Kawasaki disease may present with unilateral cervical adenopathy. Features suggesting malignancy, such as lymphoma or metastatic disease, include round shape, loss of the echogenic hilum, very hypoechoic or heterogeneous cortex, peripheral or chaotic vascularity, matting and supraclavicular location.
topics.whyLock: The exam wants you to separate benign, infected and suspicious nodes by morphology. Shape and hilum come first, then vascular pattern, then the clinical picture. The major practical role of ultrasound is detecting a liquefied, drainable abscess versus phlegmon, since that changes management. Trap: a supraclavicular node in a child is always concerning, even if it looks fairly normal. Another trap is calling a partly cystic branchial cleft cyst an abscessed node without recognizing its typical location.

topics.title: Normal Thymus
topics.frontClue: A soft, starry-sky organ in the infant chest that drapes around vessels without pushing them
topics.corePiece: The thymus is a lymphoid organ in the anterior superior mediastinum that is relatively large in infants and young children and involutes after puberty. On chest radiographs it can mimic a mass or cardiomegaly, producing the sail sign, so ultrasound is often used to confirm that a widened mediastinum is normal thymus. It is imaged through suprasternal, parasternal and sometimes subxiphoid windows with a linear or small curvilinear transducer. The normal thymus is homogeneous, with echogenicity similar to or slightly less than liver or spleen, and contains fine echogenic linear strands and dots that create a starry-sky appearance. It is soft and pliable; it changes shape with respiration and conforms to adjacent structures, draping around the great vessels and heart without compressing or displacing them. Normal flow is present without mass effect. The thymus shrinks rapidly with stress, illness or steroids and may rebound afterward. Ectopic cervical thymus can appear as a neck mass with the same echotexture and continuity with the mediastinal thymus.
topics.whyLock: The goal is to recognize normal tissue and avoid unnecessary CT. Normal thymus has a consistent echotexture, molds to vessels, and never compresses the airway or vessels. Features that should raise concern for an anterior mediastinal mass, such as lymphoma or a germ cell tumor, include heterogeneous echotexture, calcification, cystic components, displacement of vessels or airway, and a lobulated contour. Trap: assuming a small thymus in a sick infant is abnormal; it is often stress involution.

topics.title: Pediatric Pleural Effusion
topics.frontClue: Fluid above the diaphragm: septations mean a complicated effusion that may need drainage
topics.corePiece: Ultrasound is ideal for pleural assessment in children because it is portable, radiation-free and better than radiographs at characterizing fluid. Scan from below the costal margin or through intercostal spaces with the child sitting, supine or decubitus, using a curved or linear transducer. A pleural effusion is fluid between the visceral and parietal pleura above the diaphragm. Normally the spine is not seen above the diaphragm because aerated lung blocks it; with an effusion or consolidation the spine is visible above the diaphragm, the spine sign. Simple effusions are anechoic, but anechoic fluid can be either transudate or exudate. Echogenic fluid, swirling particles, septations, loculations and pleural thickening indicate an exudate and suggest a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Consolidated lung appears hepatized, tissue-like, with dynamic air bronchograms that move with respiration, separating pneumonia from atelectasis. Ultrasound guides thoracentesis and chest tube placement and identifies septations that may favor fibrinolytic therapy or thoracoscopic surgery.
topics.whyLock: Characterize, then quantify. Septations and loculations change management because simple drainage may fail. The key trap is assuming anechoic fluid is a transudate; many early exudates are anechoic. Another trap is mistaking consolidated lung or the spleen for fluid. In neonates, chylothorax is a common cause of isolated effusion, and in older children, parapneumonic effusion dominates. Always image the opposite side and the pericardium, and document fluid depth so serial exams can be compared.

topics.title: Pediatric Tumor Overview
topics.frontClue: Match the tumor to the organ and the age: a map of pediatric malignancy
topics.corePiece: Leukemia is the most common childhood cancer overall, followed by central nervous system tumors. Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor and the most common malignancy of infancy. Organizing tumors by location and age helps on the exam. Kidney: Wilms tumor peaks at 3 to 4 years; mesoblastic nephroma is the most common solid renal mass in the neonate; renal cell carcinoma appears in adolescents. Adrenal: neuroblastoma. Liver: infantile hemangioma under 6 months, hepatoblastoma in children under 3, hepatocellular carcinoma in teens. Pelvis: rhabdomyosarcoma of the bladder, prostate or vagina, the grape-like sarcoma botryoides; sacrococcygeal teratoma, the most common neonatal tumor, arising from the coccyx with cystic and solid components. Ovary: germ cell tumors dominate, with mature cystic teratoma the most common ovarian neoplasm in children, showing an echogenic Rokitansky nodule and shadowing. Testis: teratoma and yolk sac tumor before puberty. Mediastinum and nodes: lymphoma. Soft tissue: rhabdomyosarcoma. Tumor markers include AFP for hepatoblastoma and yolk sac tumor and urine catecholamines for neuroblastoma.
topics.whyLock: Many exam questions can be answered with only the age, organ and marker. A neonate with a solid renal mass has mesoblastic nephroma, not Wilms. A 2-year-old with a calcified adrenal mass and high catecholamines has neuroblastoma. A girl with abdominal pain and a calcified adnexal mass with an echogenic plug has a teratoma. Trap: forgetting that physiologic AFP is very high in newborns. Remember also that ultrasound documents organ of origin, vascular involvement and metastases, especially to the liver.

topics.title: Pediatric Preparation & Sedation
topics.frontClue: Short fasts, warm gel, and sedation only rarely for ultrasound
topics.corePiece: Preparation is tailored to age and exam. For gallbladder and biliary imaging, a fast of about 3 to 4 hours is typical in infants and about 4 to 6 hours in older children, balanced against hypoglycemia risk; biliary atresia studies usually use about 4 hours. Pyloric exams need no fasting, and a feed of clear fluid can help. Pelvic exams require a full bladder by drinking fluids or, rarely, by catheter in a child who cannot cooperate. Neonatal intensive care exams are done at the bedside, often through incubator portholes, with warmed gel, minimal exposure, strict hand hygiene and transducer disinfection, and attention to lines, leads and monitors. Sedation is rarely needed for ultrasound because it is painless and can be paused. When sedation is used, for example for Doppler or long procedures, it requires a physician order, fasting according to institutional guidelines, continuous monitoring including pulse oximetry, trained staff and resuscitation equipment.
topics.whyLock: Fasting reasons matter: a contracted gallbladder after feeding can mimic wall thickening or an absent gallbladder in suspected biliary atresia, but over-fasting a neonate is unsafe. Thermoregulation is a major risk in premature infants, so keep them covered and warm. Infection control is essential in the NICU because these infants are immunocompromised. Trap: offering sedation as a default rather than using distraction, feeding and patience. If sedation is used, the sonographer must recognize respiratory depression and know who to call.

topics.title: Child-Friendly Technique & Transducer Selection
topics.frontClue: Small patient, high frequency: linear for surface, small curved for depth
topics.corePiece: Children have less body fat and smaller dimensions, so higher frequencies can be used for better resolution. A high-frequency linear transducer, about 9 to 18 MHz, is the workhorse for the pylorus, appendix and bowel, intussusception, scrotum, hips, spine, neck, soft tissues and the superficial liver in infants. A small-footprint curved or microconvex transducer of about 5 to 9 MHz suits the infant and child abdomen and pelvis, and a low-frequency curved array is used in larger adolescents. A sector or microconvex probe fits the fontanelles and intercostal spaces. Technique is age-appropriate: let a parent stay, explain what will happen in simple words, warm the gel, use toys, videos, songs or bubbles for distraction, and give infants a bottle or pacifier. Use a child life specialist when available. Start with the least threatening area and the most important images first, because cooperation may be brief. Keep imaging pressure gentle, especially over a painful abdomen, and adjust depth, focus and gain to the small field of view.
topics.whyLock: The principle is that resolution and cooperation both drive diagnostic quality. A crying child creates bowel gas, motion and an abdomen too tense to compress, so investing in comfort saves time. Know the order of priorities so that the critical images are captured early. Traps include using a large adult curved probe on a neonate, which wastes resolution, and forgetting that frequency must drop in obese adolescents. Never restrain a child forcefully; involve parents and staff and follow institutional policies.

topics.title: Non-Accidental Trauma Awareness
topics.frontClue: Injuries that do not fit the story: document objectively and report per policy
topics.corePiece: Non-accidental trauma, or child abuse, should be considered when injuries are inconsistent with the history or the child's developmental stage, when injuries of different ages are present, or when care was delayed. Infants and young children are most at risk. Abdominal injuries are a leading cause of death in abused children and include liver and splenic lacerations, duodenal hematoma, pancreatic injury with pancreatitis or pseudocyst, and bowel perforation, particularly in toddlers without a clear mechanism. Cranial sonography can detect extra-axial fluid or parenchymal injury in infants with an open fontanelle, but CT and MRI are needed for head trauma, and ultrasound does not exclude intracranial injury. Skeletal surveys remain the standard for fractures; ultrasound may show cortical disruption or periosteal reaction. The sonographer's role is to document findings objectively with labeled images and measurements, avoid accusatory comments, preserve privacy, and communicate concerns to the interpreting physician. Healthcare workers are mandated reporters in all US states and must follow institutional reporting policies.
topics.whyLock: The registry tests awareness and professional behavior more than diagnosis. Patterns raise suspicion: duodenal hematoma or pancreatitis in a toddler, injuries of different ages, and history that changes. The trap is acting outside scope, such as confronting caregivers or discussing suspicions with the family. Document carefully, include both sides, and report through the proper channel. Another trap is assuming a normal head ultrasound excludes inflicted injury; it does not, and CT or MRI is required.

topics.title: ALARA in Children
topics.frontClue: No ionizing radiation, but still as low as reasonably achievable: watch TI, MI and Doppler time
topics.corePiece: Ultrasound is preferred in children because it uses no ionizing radiation, but it deposits energy and the ALARA principle, as low as reasonably achievable, still applies. Two on-screen indices guide safety. The thermal index estimates potential temperature rise: TIS for soft tissue, TIB when bone lies at or near the focus, as in the fetal or neonatal skull and spine, and TIC when bone is at the skin surface. The mechanical index estimates the potential for cavitation and nonthermal effects and is most relevant where gas is present, such as lung and bowel. Spectral and color Doppler generally produce higher intensities and higher TI than grayscale, so keep Doppler time short, especially in the neonatal head and over ossifying bone. Practical steps include starting with a low output power and increasing receiver gain before increasing output, minimizing dwell time, using freeze when not actively scanning, choosing appropriate presets for pediatric and neonatal exams, and avoiding nondiagnostic or entertainment scanning. Exam time should match clinical need.
topics.whyLock: Remember that gain amplifies received signals without increasing patient exposure, while output power increases exposure, so gain is the first adjustment when images are dark. Thermal effects increase with dwell time, bone absorption and Doppler, and infants have limited ability to dissipate heat. Trap: assuming no radiation means no risk. Another trap is choosing TIS for a scan where bone lies at the focus. Pediatric presets reduce default output and are an easy safety habit.
